title: Electrophilic aromatic substitution
goal: How arenes react with electrophiles, and where.

problemSets.title: Making the electrophile
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Benzene is a weak nucleophile: it needs a strong electrophile, made first.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Aromatic rings only react with **strong** electrophiles. Each reaction here makes one:

- **NO₂⁺** from nitric acid, protonated by sulfuric acid
- **Br⁺** (as Br–Br–AlBr₃) and **R⁺** or **RC≡O⁺** with a Lewis acid, AlX₃, taking a halide

Watch for carbocations that **rearrange** before the ring ever sees them.

setItems.whyThisOne: Proton transfer, then loss of water: NO₂⁺.
A Lewis acid polarises Br₂ in one arrow.
An oxygen lone pair stabilises the cation: no rearrangement.
A hydride shift: the primary cation never forms.

problemSets.title: The arenium ion
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: An electrophile adds, the arenium ion loses H⁺, aromaticity returns.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Every reaction in this set has the same two steps.

1. A ring **π bond attacks** the electrophile. Aromaticity is lost: the **arenium (Wheland) ion** carries the positive charge on three ring carbons. This is the slow step.
2. A base (the counter-ion) **removes the H⁺** from the sp³ carbon and the ring is aromatic again.

Substitution, not addition: losing H⁺ restores aromaticity.

setItems.whyThisOne: The pattern with the nitronium ion.
The Lewis acid leaves with the bromide and comes back.
The rearrangement trap: isopropyl, not propyl.
Acylation stops after one: the ketone deactivates.
A neutral electrophile, SO₃, and a final proton transfer.

problemSets.title: Directing effects
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Donors direct ortho/para, withdrawing groups direct meta: follow the positive charge.
problemSets.conceptCard:
After attack, draw where the **positive charge** goes. Ortho or para attack puts it, in one resonance form, on the carbon **bearing the substituent**.

- A **donor** (CH₃, OMe, OH, NHCOR, even Cl) stabilises that form: **ortho/para**.
- A **withdrawing group** (NO₂, C=O) makes that form very bad, so **meta** wins.

OH and OMe also **activate** the ring; halogens deactivate but still direct ortho/para.

setItems.whyThisOne: A tertiary carbocation form; ortho and para both form.
The oxygen lone pair gives an oxocarbenium form.
So activated that no Lewis acid is needed.
A nitrogen donor, tamed by the carbonyl.
Deactivating, yet ortho/para.
The meta director: the charge avoids the nitro carbon.

problemSets.title: Predict the position
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: New substrates: decide donor or withdrawing first, then attack.
problemSets.conceptCard:
No resonance steps are drawn here: decide the position **before** you draw.

Ask: does the group **donate** a lone pair or σ electrons (ortho/para), or **withdraw** through a C=O or N⁺ (meta)? For a bulky electrophile, prefer **para** over ortho.

setItems.whyThisOne: An activated ring: Br₂ alone.
An ester: meta.
A bulky electrophile: para.
Ortho and para both count.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Make the electrophile, attack in the right place, restore the ring.
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: Making an electrophile.
The basic pattern.
Which carbon ends up on the ring?
Deactivating but ortho/para.
